item.description:
How Colombia's budget cuts threaten a key human rights court
President Abelardo de la Espriella has pledged to slash spending on JEP, Colombia's transitional justice court. But war crimes victims fear the cost.The Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) is a transitional justice court in Bogota, Colombia, that handles cases of war crimes and other conflict-related abuses [File: Luisa Gonzalez/Reuters]Colombian Magistrate Alejandro Ramelli of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) speaks during a sentencing on September 18, 2025 [File: Luisa Gonzalez/Reuters]By Daniela Diaz Rangel and Joshua CollinsPublished On 30 Oct 202630 Oct 2026

Bogota, Colombia – Angela Cordon was only a teenager when her father and uncle disappeared.
They were among a string of farmers and merchants to go missing in the southwestern department of Huila in Colombia.
First came her uncle Reynaldo Cordon Herrera's kidnapping. A grocer by trade, he had been travelling by truck on January 22, 2003, when he went missing.
The next month, Guillermo Cordon Herrera — Angela's father — set out to discover what happened to his brother, tracing his whereabouts through rural Colombia.
Guillermo called home one night with news: He had made contact with the rebel fighters he believed to be responsible for his brother's abduction.
It was the last time his family would ever hear from him. His body was never found, nor was his brother's.
Angela's father and uncle are among the more than 450,664 people killed as part of Colombia's six-decade-long internal armed conflict.
In the 23 years since their disappearance, Angela and her family have sought any information they could find about their loved ones' last days. "I have dedicated my life to this search," she told Al Jazeera.

A years-long, paid-for influence operation promoting racist, Islamophobic and anti-Qatar views has been uncovered by two academics, with the evidence suggesting the campaign was intended to serve Israeli interests.
The investigation, which took three years, was published on Thursday. It detailed an operation that likely cost more than $11m and was carried out across 30 countries, including in Europe, the United States and Lebanon.

As part of the campaign, several million internet users were exposed to advertisements on sites like YouTube, TikTok and Facebook that pushed an agenda, according to the report titled Manufacturing the “Great Replacement”.
Marc Owen Jones, a professor at Northwestern University’s Doha campus, and independent researcher Sohan Dsouza, the academics who published the report, called it “perhaps one of the biggest digital influence and disinformation operations ever documented”.
Their report uncovered at least 533 million exposures of social media advertisements promoting anti-Muslim, anti-migrant, racist and anti-Qatar views between October 2023 and October 2026. It added that the advertisements were launched ahead of elections in some of the target countries.

Switzerland has formally reopened its diplomatic office in North Korea as Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis held talks in Pyongyang about normalising political relations between the two countries.
On Friday Cassis wrapped up a two-day visit to North Korea – the first by a Swiss government minister in more than two decades – in which he discussed “regularising political relations and reestablishing a political dialogue”, he wrote on X.

“We also exchanged views on security on the Korean Peninsula and broader Eurasian security challenges,” he added on X.
After the formal reopening of the Swiss diplomatic office on Thursday, Cassis posted that he was “pleased” to mark a “new chapter” in his country’s presence in Pyongyang, hailing the office as a “concrete step towards strengthening direct dialogue” with North Korea.

A day after announcing he would cancel a pair of campaign rallies, United States President Donald Trump has reversed course, opting to put those events back on the calendar.
A source close to the Trump administration told Al Jazeera on Friday that Trump will be headlining, in person, the previously cancelled rallies in Kansas and Iowa ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

“Rallies are BACK ON!” the source said. “No one works harder, fights harder, or loves the American people more than President Donald J. Trump!”
Previously, Trump was due to travel to Kansas on Saturday and Iowa on Sunday. But now both rallies will take place on Sunday.
The source said the events were rearranged to include more tele-rallies, which allow Trump to attend virtually.
Republican officials have also not ruled out that an additional campaign event could be added to the president’s schedule before the midterm election.
The decision marks a sharp reversal after Trump told reporters on Thursday, “I don’t feel I have to go to Kansas.”
“We are going to have a strong ⁠Tuesday night,” Trump said of the midterms.
